#### Overview

This tutorial develops a complete clinical prediction-modeling workflow using the `NHANES` R package and diabetes as the binary outcome.

The workflow covers:

1. Research question and target population
2. Data import and data dictionary

10. Logistic regression model development
11. Interaction assessment
12. Model-selection approaches
13. Penalized regression with LASSO
14. Apparent model performance
15. Bootstrap internal validation
16. Discrimination
17. Calibration
18. Brier score
19. Decision-curve analysis
20. Threshold-based classification performance
21. Sensitivity analyses
22. Subgroup performance
23. Temporal validation using NHANES survey cycles
24. Recalibration
25. Individual prediction
26. Nomogram
27. Recommended reporting framework

> **Important:** `NHANES::NHANES` is a teaching dataset derived from NHANES. This example predicts **prevalent diabetes at the time of survey**, not future incident diabetes. For a publication-quality NHANES analysis, use the original CDC NHANES files and account for the complex survey design, weights, strata, and PSU variables.

#### 2. Research Question

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This subsection explains **2. Research Question** and shows how it contributes to the overall NHANES Diabetes Prediction: Complete Clinical Prediction Modeling Workflow in R workflow.


We want to predict whether an adult participant has diabetes using demographic, anthropometric, blood-pressure, lipid, and lifestyle information.

The binary outcome is

\[
Y_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{Diabetes = Yes} \\
0, & \text{Diabetes = No}
\end{cases}
\]

The candidate predictor set is

\[
\text{Age} + \text{BMI} + \text{BPSysAve} + \text{TotChol} +
\text{Gender} + \text{Race1} + \text{PhysActive} + \text{Smoke100}.
\]

We deliberately **do not use `DiabetesAge`**, because it is downstream of diabetes diagnosis and would create outcome leakage.

#### 4. Create the Initial Analysis Dataset

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This section prepares the information needed for **4. Create the Initial Analysis Dataset**. Check variable definitions, units, coding, and missing values before moving to analysis.


We restrict the example to adults aged 20 years or older and participants with a defined diabetes outcome.


<!-- generated-learning-note -->
**Purpose.** This block prepares the analysis data. Follow each transformation carefully because filtering, recoding, grouping, and reshaping determine the observations used downstream.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nhanes0 <- NHANES %>%
  select(all_of(required_vars))

nhanes1 <- nhanes0 %>%
  filter(
    Age >= 20,
    Diabetes %in% c("Yes", "No")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Diabetes_num = if_else(Diabetes == "Yes", 1L, 0L)
  )

cat("Adult analytical cohort N =", nrow(nhanes1), "\n")
```

#### 8.1 IQR flagging for BMI

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This subsection explains **8.1 IQR flagging for BMI** and shows how it contributes to the overall NHANES Diabetes Prediction: Complete Clinical Prediction Modeling Workflow in R workflow.



<!-- generated-learning-note -->
**Purpose.** This block prepares the analysis data. Follow each transformation carefully because filtering, recoding, grouping, and reshaping determine the observations used downstream.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
q1_bmi <- quantile(nhanes1$BMI, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
q3_bmi <- quantile(nhanes1$BMI, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
iqr_bmi <- q3_bmi - q1_bmi

bmi_lower <- q1_bmi - 1.5 * iqr_bmi
bmi_upper <- q3_bmi + 1.5 * iqr_bmi

bmi_outliers <- nhanes1 %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(BMI),
    BMI < bmi_lower | BMI > bmi_upper
  ) %>%
  select(ID, Age, Gender, BMI, Diabetes)

head(bmi_outliers, 20)
```

#### 26. Decision-Curve Analysis

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This section uses **26. Decision-Curve Analysis** to make patterns visible. Confirm what each axis, group, scale, and annotation represents.


To avoid dependence on an additional package, this tutorial calculates net benefit directly.

For a threshold probability \(p_t\), net benefit is

\[
NB = \frac{TP}{N} - \frac{FP}{N}\frac{p_t}{1-p_t}.
\]

#### 26.1 Function to calculate model net benefit

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This section develops **26.1 Function to calculate model net benefit**. Read the model specification together with its assumptions and the scale of each reported effect.



<!-- generated-learning-note -->
**Purpose.** This block defines a reusable function. Separate its inputs, calculations, and returned value before applying it to new data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
net_benefit_model <- function(y, p, threshold) {
  pred_positive <- p >= threshold

  tp <- sum(pred_positive & y == 1)
  fp <- sum(pred_positive & y == 0)
  n <- length(y)

  tp / n - fp / n * threshold / (1 - threshold)
}

net_benefit_all <- function(y, threshold) {
  prevalence <- mean(y)
  prevalence - (1 - prevalence) * threshold / (1 - threshold)
}
```
:::


<!-- generated-learning-note -->
**How to read the output.** Test the function with simple inputs whose expected answer is known before relying on it in a larger workflow.

Factor levels can differ in capitalization across datasets. The following helper selects an available level using case-insensitive matching.


<!-- generated-learning-note -->
**Purpose.** This block defines a reusable function. Separate its inputs, calculations, and returned value before applying it to new data.

```{.r .cell-code}
match_factor_level <- function(x, desired) {
  lvls <- levels(x)
  idx <- match(tolower(desired), tolower(lvls))

  if (is.na(idx)) {
    stop(
      "Requested level '", desired,
      "' not found. Available levels: ",
      paste(lvls, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  lvls[idx]
}
```

For a real publication, consider the following upgrades beyond this teaching example:

2. Account for NHANES sampling weights, strata, and PSU structure when the research question targets population inference.
3. Prespecify predictors based on clinical knowledge and prior literature.

6. Use nonlinear modeling when clinically/statistically justified.

8. Preserve the complete model-building algorithm inside every bootstrap resample, including variable selection if variable selection is part of the algorithm.
9. Report optimism-corrected discrimination and calibration.

11. Report according to current prediction-model reporting guidance applicable to the study.
12. Keep data-cleaning, derivation, modeling, validation, and reporting code reproducible and version controlled.
